comments.value: I agree in general that the performance rating system needs a good look at, but I do feel the need to point out that 1ms is almost 10% of a frame at 90fps, and about 14% at 144fps. That's quite significant, especially for VR headset users, when you consider that a room may have several similar-performing avatars.

@{62e1338f5d95dd469bfc8f94|full_name}: For an entire avatar? That is very good performance.  Most avatars are like 6-10ms unless they're quest-level avatars using unlit shaders and nothing on them (props or toggles or animations). 10% of a single frame is nothing.  Most semi-optimized avatars i run into cost like 3-5fps when i'm already at 50fps because of the damn world.  Your typical ethot costs like 10+fps.  1ms makes my avatar one of the most performing avatars in any lobby i've been in.  I've discussed these things at great length with others who also know their stuff when it comes to these things.
Expecting sub-1ms per avatar is extremely strict.  Again, you're basically expecting them to use quest avatars with a bit higher poly, which is silly.  Most of the performance killer in populated worlds, to my knowledge, is the udon safety checker that makes sure you aren't using udon to abuse peoples' avatars - but i haven't personally confirmed this (nor is it easy to test without access to now-banned debug/profiler tools).

@{5a766b8a0868b44b53569ce4|full_name}: 
1ms is not the worse performance, but it *is* quite substantial. 'Poor' performance ranking seems reasonable to me. It's totally fair to create and upload avatars like this, but users do need some control to help maintain performance for their own benefit. Headset users don't like to feel ill.
Hitting 60fps (generally regarded as the minimum by many) gives you a frame budget of 16.6ms. You could have, at most, 16 of your avatars in a blank empty space. Any more and you can't achieve 60fps. That's not terrible performance, but it's pretty mediocre, given that worlds often support more, and this doesn't include any time to render the world.
The fact that there are worse performing avatars isn't relevant to anything. The performance checker is designed to try and maintain an absolute level of good performance; it's not relative.
Performance requirements get stricter when you have users using VR headsets on PC.
Oculus link runs at 72 to 90fps, and the Index runs at 90 to 120fps (with an experimental 144hz). At 90fps, you have a 11.1ms framebudget, meaning with just 11 similar performing avatars you are likely to cause adverse effects for those users. and this is in a totally blank world. No lights or shadows or anything else that can cause your avatar to require more rending passes.
In addition to headsets having higher framerates: A jerky framerate on a monitor is a nuisance, but on a headset, it can lead to physical nausea. You will want some buffer in your budget to prevent performance spikes.
This is all on a PC, with no consideration for the Quest (which is its own unique development nightmare). This also assumes that the total performance of these avatars is simply additive, which it may not be in some circumstances (especially with per-pixel lights and VRChat's simple forward-additive lighting system). Note: additive performance between different avatars—the assumption I made above when calculating frame rates—is essentially the best-case scenario.
If I may ask, what are you doing to take up 1ms? I'm not even sure *how* I would use 1ms of frame time. My avatars performance usually registers <500ns on my 8-year-old PC, and these generally get classified as 'average' to 'good'—which I feel is fair.
There are some common misconceptions to keep in mind when optimising. For example, whereas static triangles may be cheap, triangles rigged to bones are far from it. Additionally, large numbers of dense, small triangles, regardless of if they are rigged or not, can have adverse and difficult-to-predict performance impacts based on scale and display pixel density due to how the GPU has to blend the result of the fragment shader when a pixel overlaps multiple triangle edges.

@{62e1338f5d95dd469bfc8f94|full_name}: I should have iterated that this was on an older gpu (rx580) and my cpu is subpar (r5 2600x).  Getting a world to 1ms is a miracle (someone i know put in immense efforts to achieve this).  Poiyomi on the same gpu used 0.6ms per screen-filling material, i achieved 1ms with a dozen or less materials (only like 5 active at a time) on a shader that costs 1/3 that.  Shaders are not incorporated into the system so people use very heavy shaders without cluing in, and don't notice because they are sitting rosy on their 30xx series gpu or whatever.

I haven't properly profiled CPU since physbones, but most cpu cost was on physbones and a little on mesh skinning.  GameObject count and parsing the avatar, ik etc is all goin to cost a fair bit (as having played with final ik with friends, ik is not particularly cheap).  1ms CPU bound on my cpu was an estimation including all of that and trying to counteract the overhead from the editor and scene.

My shaders are very efficient for what they can do because they are single-pass vertex-lit only, though they are very capable for what they are, and have a couple semi-costly advanced features *(performance cost could be much better, but i don't possess the technical knowledge to hyper-optimize them).*  Having compared a bunch of shaders in profile though, the only shader that is widely used that performed better was UTS2.  Mine was ～0.2-0.25ms per screen filling material, and UTS2 was 0.1ms per screen filling material, Poiyomi being at 0.6, and Xiexe at 0.25.  I never tested liltoon or others.

1ms on a 3080ti is a LOT, but 1ms on an rx480 or even rx580 is not nearly as significant.  I have a better gpu now, so profile results would be different.

About polygons - polycount is cheap even skinned, and unity caps out at 4 bones per vertex, meaning there is a performance cost limit to this.  Moving vertices with bones is not particularly expensive on render, it's just memory costly, and more bones per vertex increases this memory cost - which is why you don't rig an entire face with bones and do morphs that way because there's too many bones too close together.  As an experiment back in 2018, i took a hair with a decent amount of bones in it and smoothed it's weights a lot to make it look better, and even on my extremely dated phenom II 965 and rx480 gpu, the cost of increasing per-vertex bone deform from 2 to 4 showed no framerate impact i could measure.  The difference is mostly only if it's skinned or not (also not including batching/instancing etc).

As far as the distance thing - that's not something the end-user can solve because it requires proper LoD systems which we do not have access to, and could only be partially mitigated in shaders with *extremely advanced* work.  That goes for a number of the things you covered here, they are just impossible for users to realistically solve on their own.  Anything i've tested has significantly and consistently gone down in gpu cost as the surface moves away from the screen and reduces it's screen ratio, even on materials without LoD's.  Pretty sure the shader compiler and hardware has a lot of stuff to automatically deal with these circumstances.

ps: there is nothing absolute about the rating system.  It's values are inherently relative because the performance impact of the values presented are subjective and contextual.  for example my world has 2 spheres of identical mesh one huge and one small, both running the same shader, but the bigger one costs more performance than the smaller one, regardless of how close you shove your face in the small one *(both are static etc)*.

pps: these are editor profiles, which are not accurate to build.  we cannot profile build results because mods are now blocked, so proper profiling tools are no longer accessible.

when i said most avatars are more than 1ms by editor profile standard relative to my gpu at the time, i am pretty concrete in that.  due to the cost of the shaders they use and active material counts which usually exceed mine, there's no way they would be less than that.

these days i drop something 5-10fps per avatar in a lot of cases (and that's just from your average booth user, not talking overdone ethots), unless they are particularly simple/optimized then i can't determine any fps loss.  most people are not willing to simplify their avatars to the level of a genshin model in order to get anything below poor on the performance rating.  this makes it useless for determining which avatars are actually horrendous for performance and need serious fixing, rather than just a gradient of "which lets you have 80fps in a lobby with 70 people"...

details:
The performance checker is extremely heavy and causes significant lag spikes on initial avatar load by hogging cpu time.  There should be an option to disable the checker - some people do not care about the performance stats, especially due to the reasons i will explain.
The performance rating system misinforms the user on the true performance impact of the things it tries to measure.
* The most egregious of which is measuring the avatar's total bounds, and ignoring the fact that bounds are per gameobject, meaning having a single cube 100 miles away will not affect your avatar's performance besides running the animator at the full update rate, it will not affect the rendering of any of your skinned meshes, particles, etc, as they are individually culled.
* Another is that it overstates the impact of polygons.  Modern GPUs can run polygons like nobody's business, and you won't notice per-avatar performance impact until they get to the 200k+ polygon range (this means 200k+ enabled and rendered, not counting disabled outfits).
* Material count cost is dependant in shaders - heavy complex shaders will cause many materials to add up cost very quickly, whereas lightweight shaders (such as UTS2), you can get away with many more materials before reaching the same overhead (or even more so if you have a shader with is lit only by vertex light, like my own, meaning realtime lights do not add performance cost per material).  Due to the reality of having toggle outfits and shaders that can significantly reduce per-material cost - this is especially extraneous to properly measure.
* Vertex lights (render mode not important) are counted as lights despite having zero performance cost due to the fact that unity is always calculating all of the vertex light slots even if none are present.

If i were to add a footnote, it is that the ranking "poor, verypoor" etc is largely pointless because of inadequately measuring, which creates social conflicts over untruths about an avatar's actual performance in instances which people experience all too often.  I for example often have avatars listed as "poor or "verypoor" despite them costing a mere 1ms on GPU and ～1ms on CPU when profiled with dynamics (even on old dynamicbone).
title: Performance rating system is heavy and misinforming
